The paper proposes a systematic approach to organizing computational design workflows with heterogeneous constraints.
The approach involves classifying IP-solvers based on the properties of design constraints they can handle.
The two stages of design space in the proposed workflow are 'pruning' and 'exploration'.
Pruning provides the feasible design space for exploration.
Feasible design subspaces are described uniquely and completely by their maximal elements, which are implicitly defined by pointwise constraints.
PareTO is a Pareto-tracing levelset topology optimization method that uses fixed-point iteration to satisfy multiple design criteria guided by augmented TSFs.
PareTO can produce many alternatives on the Pareto front, some of which might satisfy additional constraints not accounted for in TO.
Traditional TO methods focus on optimizing designs for performance but less on other important factors such as manufacturability.
Considering process limitations during design/optimization can avoid repeated prototyping and iterations until the optimized designs are manufacturable.
The proposed approach for incorporating accessibility constraints in TO involves filtering the augmented TSF using the overlap measure of cutting tool and optimized part.
The limitation of the proposed approach is that it may sacrifice achieved optimality when applying corrections to the geometry or topology of a solution after TO to make it manufacturable.
The proposed workflow enables the simultaneous satisfaction of kinematics- and physics-based requirements and can produce many alternatives on the Pareto front.
The classification of solvers based on the types of constraints they can handle is based on the properties of design constraints, including locality and continuity.
The paper demonstrates the application of the proposed approach to various design problems, including topology optimization and manufacturability constraints.
The approach can be applied to real-world design problems, such as designing a car hood latch.
